# Agent Safety Rubric

<!-- Generated by `agent-scorecard rubric`. Edit the checks in src/agent_scorecard/checks, not this file. -->

27 checks across 7 layers. Each one is something you can see in a codebase, and each one closes a way that production agents actually fail.

## How scoring works

- Each check is **PASS** (2 points), **PARTIAL** (1) or **MISSING** (0). **N/A** checks are left out: sandboxing in an agent that never runs commands, file confinement where nothing writes files, and the tool and approval checks (TB-01, TB-02, AG-01 to AG-04, UI-03) and the step cap (BL-01) in a chat-only app that never calls tools.
- Points are weighted by severity: critical ×3, high ×2, medium ×1.
- A layer's score is its weighted points over the maximum possible, as a percentage.
- The overall score is the plain average of the layer scores. Defence in depth means a perfect layer can't make up for a missing one.
- Grades: A ≥ 85, B ≥ 70, C ≥ 55, D ≥ 40, otherwise F.
- **Any missing critical check caps the grade at C**, whatever the number says.

## 1. Tool boundaries

### TB-01 Tools are an explicit allowlist (high)

**Why it matters.** An agent should only see the tools its job needs. Handing it every tool a library or MCP server exposes turns one bad prompt into access to all of them.

**What the scanner looks for.** allowed_tools / allowedTools / disallowed_tools (Claude Agent SDK), MCP tool filters (include_tools, tool_filter), named tool allowlists; weaker: explicit tools=[...] lists, @tool / @function_tool / server.tool() declarations.

- **Pass:** Tool access is filtered through an allowlist or denylist.
- **Partial:** Tools are declared explicitly, but nothing filters which ones an agent may call.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Give each agent or role an allowlist of tool names and load only those. For MCP, filter the server's tools rather than exposing all of them.

### TB-02 Tools carry a risk tier (critical)

**Why it matters.** Approval, logging and budgets all depend on knowing which tools only read and which change the world. Without tiers, every safety layer has to guess.

**What the scanner looks for.** risk_level / security_risk / ToolTier / read_only / readOnlyHint / destructiveHint / requires_confirmation on tool definitions.

- **Pass:** Tools are classified by risk in code (read-only, side-effecting, destructive).
- **Partial:** Some tools are named as dangerous or side-effecting, without a systematic tier.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Add a tier to every tool (read, write, irreversible) and make approvals and budgets key off it. MCP's readOnlyHint and destructiveHint are a good minimum.

### TB-03 Code and shell execution is sandboxed (critical)

**Why it matters.** If an agent can run commands, a prompt injection can too. Isolation decides whether that is an annoyance or a breach.

**What the scanner looks for.** subprocess / child_process / exec.Command / eval paths, and alongside them a sandbox (Docker, E2B, Modal, gVisor, nsjail, seccomp) or at least a command allowlist and shell=False. N/A when the code never executes commands.

- **Pass:** Execution runs inside a sandbox or container.
- **Partial:** Commands are restricted (allowlist, shlex, shell=False) but not isolated.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Run agent-issued commands in a throwaway container or microVM with no host credentials and no default network, and keep an allowlist on top.

### TB-04 File access is confined to a workspace (high)

**Why it matters.** Agents that read or write files can be steered to ../../.ssh or to overwrite their own config. A single path check closes most of that.

**What the scanner looks for.** is_relative_to / commonpath / safe_join / secure_filename / filepath.Rel / workspace-root checks next to file writes. N/A when nothing writes or deletes files.

- **Pass:** Paths are resolved and checked against an allowed root.
- **Partial:** Paths are normalised (realpath/abspath), but no root check was found.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Resolve every path the agent supplies and reject it unless it sits under the workspace root. Test it with ../ and symlink cases.

### TB-05 Tool supply chain is pinned (medium)

**Why it matters.** Tools are code the agent runs with your credentials. An unpinned `npx -y some-mcp` pulls whatever was published five minutes ago.

**What the scanner looks for.** A lockfile covering every dependency manifest (same or parent directory, so workspaces count), and MCP server entries pinned to a version or image digest instead of `npx -y pkg` or `:latest`. Examples and tests are ignored.

- **Pass:** Dependencies are locked and every MCP server is pinned.
- **Partial:** Some manifests are locked, or MCP servers float while dependencies are locked.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Commit lockfiles, pin MCP servers to exact versions (pkg@1.2.3, image@sha256:…) and update them deliberately.

## 2. Human approval gates

### AG-01 Side effects wait for human approval (critical)

**Why it matters.** The one control that stops a confused or hijacked agent before it sends, pays, deletes or deploys. Everything else only tells you afterwards.

**What the scanner looks for.** LangGraph interrupt() / interrupt_before, CrewAI human_input=True, Claude Agent SDK can_use_tool or PreToolUse hooks, OpenAI Agents needs_approval, or an approval request/queue/policy of the project's own.

- **Pass:** A real gate pauses the agent for a human decision on risky actions.
- **Partial:** Approval or confirmation is mentioned in code, but no blocking gate was found.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Put a gate in front of every side-effecting tool tier: the agent proposes, a human approves the exact action, and only then does it run.

### AG-02 Approvals are bound to the exact action (high)

**Why it matters.** An approval that says 'yes' without pinning what was approved can be replayed or swapped for a different payload between the click and the call.

**What the scanner looks for.** In approval code: a signature or hash of the action (hmac, sha256, digest, nonce) and an expiry (expires_at, ttl).

- **Pass:** Approvals are signed or hashed over the action and expire.
- **Partial:** Approvals carry either an integrity check or an expiry, not both.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Store the proposed action, sign or hash it with the approval id, give it a short expiry, and re-check both right before execution.

### AG-03 The gate fails closed (critical)

**Why it matters.** Gates break in boring ways: a timeout, a missing tier, an env var left on from a demo. If the default is 'allow', the gate is decoration.

**What the scanner looks for.** Anti-patterns in production code: bypassPermissions, auto_approve=True, --yolo, confirmation_mode=False. Good signs: deny-by-default, reject on timeout or expiry, unknown tools denied.

- **Pass:** Defaults deny, and nothing in production code switches approvals off.
- **Partial:** A gate exists and no bypass was found, but its failure default is not visible.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Make deny the default on timeout, error and unknown tools. Keep bypass modes out of production code paths, behind an explicit, logged, test-only flag.

### AG-04 Approval decisions are recorded (high)

**Why it matters.** When something goes wrong the first question is 'who approved this, and what did they see?'. That answer has to exist before the incident.

**What the scanner looks for.** approved_by / approver_id / decided_by / decision records / an approvals table, and approved_at or decision timestamps.

- **Pass:** Each decision stores who decided and when.
- **Partial:** Decisions are stored, but without who made them.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Persist every approval and rejection with approver identity, timestamp, the exact action shown and the outcome.

## 3. Audit trail and observability

### AU-01 Every tool call is logged as a structured event (high)

**Why it matters.** Agents fail in ways nobody predicted. A structured record of each tool call, its arguments and its result is the only way to find out what actually happened.

**What the scanner looks for.** Audit log/event types, tool-call callbacks (on_tool_start/on_tool_end), action and observation events; weaker: plain application logging.

- **Pass:** Tool calls are written to a dedicated audit or event log.
- **Partial:** General logging only; tool calls are not recorded as their own events.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Emit one structured event per tool call (agent, tool, args digest, result status, approval id, cost) to an audit sink separate from debug logs.

### AU-02 Runs are traced end to end (medium)

**Why it matters.** A trace ties the prompt, every model call, every tool call and the cost of one run together, which is what you need to debug and to price the product.

**What the scanner looks for.** Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry, Logfire, Helicone, Arize Phoenix, AgentOps, Braintrust, Laminar, Weave or Traceloop in code, config or dependencies; weaker: trace or correlation ids.

- **Pass:** An LLM tracing or OpenTelemetry integration is wired in.
- **Partial:** Trace or correlation ids exist, but no tracing backend.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Wire one tracing backend and propagate a run id through every model and tool call.

### AU-03 The audit trail is durable and tamper-evident (medium)

**Why it matters.** A log the agent (or an attacker using it) can edit is not evidence. Regulated buyers will ask how you know the record is complete.

**What the scanner looks for.** append-only storage, hash chaining (prev_hash), object lock / WORM, or immutability notes; weaker: audit events persisted to a database or file.

- **Pass:** Audit records are append-only or hash-chained.
- **Partial:** Audit events are persisted, but nothing makes them tamper-evident.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Write audit events append-only (separate table with insert-only grants, or object lock), and chain each record to the previous hash.

### AU-04 Secrets are redacted from logs and traces (high)

**Why it matters.** Agents see tokens in tool arguments and results. Without redaction, the audit log becomes the easiest place to steal them from.

**What the scanner looks for.** redact / scrub / mask_secret / SecretStr / REDACTED helpers in logging or tracing code.

- **Pass:** A redaction step strips secrets before logging or tracing.
- **Partial:** Secrets are wrapped in secret types, but no redaction of log output was found.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Run every logged payload through a redactor (known keys plus token patterns) and test it with real-looking secrets.

## 4. Secrets and egress

### SE-01 No secrets are committed (critical)

**Why it matters.** A key in the repo is a key in every clone, fork and CI log. Agents make it worse: they read the repo and can paste the key anywhere.

**What the scanner looks for.** Provider key formats (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS, GitHub, Slack, Google, Stripe), private keys, and long literal values assigned to api_key / token / password, plus committed .env files. Matches are redacted in the report.

- **Pass:** Nothing that looks like a live secret is committed.
- **Partial:** Secret-shaped values appear only in tests or examples; confirm they are fake.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Rotate anything found, move it to the environment or a secret manager, and purge it from history.

### SE-02 Secrets come from the environment or a vault (high)

**Why it matters.** Keys loaded at runtime can be rotated, scoped per environment and kept out of the model's context. Keys in code can't.

**What the scanner looks for.** os.environ / getenv / process.env / pydantic BaseSettings / a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, SSM, Vault, GCP Secret Manager, keyring), plus .env in .gitignore.

- **Pass:** Secrets are read at runtime and .env files are git-ignored.
- **Partial:** Secrets are read from the environment, but .env is not git-ignored.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Load secrets through one settings module, git-ignore .env, and ship a .env.example.

### SE-03 Secret scanning runs before merge (medium)

**Why it matters.** People and agents both paste keys. A scanner in CI or pre-commit catches it before it reaches the default branch.

**What the scanner looks for.** gitleaks, trufflehog, detect-secrets, ggshield, secretlint or git-secrets in CI or pre-commit; weaker: other static security scanners (CodeQL, Semgrep, Bandit).

- **Pass:** A secret scanner runs in CI or pre-commit.
- **Partial:** Static security scanning runs, but no dedicated secret scanner.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Add gitleaks or trufflehog to CI and pre-commit, and fail the build on findings.

### SE-04 Outbound network access is restricted (high)

**Why it matters.** Exfiltration needs somewhere to send data. An agent that can fetch any URL can be told to send your data to any URL.

**What the scanner looks for.** Domain or host allowlists for fetch/browse tools, private-IP and SSRF blocking, egress policies (NetworkPolicy, firewall rules); weaker: denylists.

- **Pass:** Fetch and browse tools are limited to an allowlist, or private ranges are blocked.
- **Partial:** Some destinations are denied, but the default is open.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Route agent HTTP through one client with a domain allowlist, block private and metadata IPs, and deny network by default in sandboxes.

## 5. Budgets and limits

### BL-01 Agent loops have a step cap (critical)

**Why it matters.** Agents loop: they retry, re-plan and call each other. Without a hard cap, one bad task becomes thousands of model and tool calls.

**What the scanner looks for.** recursion_limit (LangGraph), max_iter / max_rpm (CrewAI), max_turns (Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents), max_steps / max_iterations / max_tool_calls of the project's own. N/A in a chat-only app with no tool loop.

- **Pass:** Agent runs stop after a bounded number of steps.
- **Partial:** Only retries are bounded; the agent loop itself is not.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Set a step cap on every agent loop, make hitting it a visible failure, and alert on it.

### BL-02 Spend has a budget (high)

**Why it matters.** Model spend is the bill nobody sees until month end. A per-run or per-tenant budget turns a runaway agent into an error instead of an invoice.

**What the scanner looks for.** max_budget_usd, budget/cost/spend limits, quotas, usage limits, BudgetExceeded; weaker: cost or token tracking without a limit, or only max_tokens per call.

- **Pass:** Runs or tenants have an enforced cost or token budget.
- **Partial:** Cost or tokens are tracked, or capped per call, but nothing enforces a budget.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Track cost per run and per tenant, stop the run when it crosses a budget, and show spend next to every run.

### BL-03 Model and tool calls time out (high)

**Why it matters.** A hung tool call holds a worker, a lock and sometimes an approval slot forever. Timeouts are what make the other limits enforceable.

**What the scanner looks for.** timeout= arguments, asyncio.wait_for / asyncio.timeout, context.WithTimeout, AbortSignal.timeout, request_timeout across several files.

- **Pass:** Timeouts are set on calls in several places.
- **Partial:** A timeout appears in only one place.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Give every model call, tool call and external request a timeout, and make the agent treat a timeout as a failed step.

## 6. Untrusted input handling

### UI-01 Untrusted content is marked as data (critical)

**Why it matters.** Web pages, emails, files and tool results can carry instructions. If the prompt doesn't separate them from yours, the model can't either. This is prompt injection.

**What the scanner looks for.** Code that labels external content as untrusted, prompt-injection defences, guardrail libraries (LLM Guard, NeMo Guardrails, Rebuff, Lakera, Prompt Guard); weaker: wrapping external content in tags such as <document> or <search_results>.

- **Pass:** External content is labelled untrusted or screened before it reaches the model.
- **Partial:** External content is wrapped in delimiters, or prompt injection is acknowledged in code, but content is not labelled or screened.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Wrap every piece of external content in a labelled block, tell the model it is data, never instructions, screen it, and keep tool tiers enforced whatever it says.

### UI-02 Model output is parsed into a schema (high)

**Why it matters.** Free text that later drives a tool call or a database write is where hallucinated and injected values slip through. A schema rejects them at the boundary.

**What the scanner looks for.** with_structured_output, response_format / json_schema, output_pydantic, output_type, PydanticOutputParser, Zod schemas, instructor; weaker: bare json.loads / JSON.parse of model text.

- **Pass:** Model output that drives actions is validated against a schema.
- **Partial:** Model output is parsed as JSON without a schema.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Request structured output and validate it with Pydantic or Zod before anything acts on it.

### UI-03 Tool arguments are validated (high)

**Why it matters.** The model writes the arguments. Types, ranges and formats are the last check before they hit a shell, a query or an API.

**What the scanner looks for.** args_schema, input_schema / inputSchema, Pydantic models with constraints, validate_call, jsonschema.validate, Zod; weaker: typed tool functions only.

- **Pass:** Tool inputs are checked against explicit schemas or constraints.
- **Partial:** Tools are typed, but inputs are not validated beyond that.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Give every tool a schema with constraints (enums, lengths, patterns) and reject anything outside it before execution.

## 7. Evals, testing and rollback

### ER-01 Tests exist and run in CI (high)

**Why it matters.** An agent's safety layers are code. Untested code drifts, and a gate that silently stopped gating is worse than no gate.

**What the scanner looks for.** Test files, and a CI workflow that runs them.

- **Pass:** A test suite runs in CI.
- **Partial:** Tests exist but CI doesn't run them, or CI exists without tests.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Run the test suite on every pull request and block merges on failure.

### ER-02 Agent behaviour has evals (high)

**Why it matters.** Unit tests check code; evals check behaviour. A prompt or model change can pass every unit test and still make the agent worse or less safe.

**What the scanner looks for.** An evals/ or benchmarks/ directory, eval frameworks (promptfoo, deepeval, ragas, Inspect, LangSmith evaluate, Braintrust, OpenAI evals), datasets of cases; weaker: golden files, LLM-as-judge helpers.

- **Pass:** Agent behaviour is measured against an eval set.
- **Partial:** Golden files or LLM-judge helpers exist, but no eval suite.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Keep a small eval set of real tasks (including unsafe ones) and run it on every prompt, tool or model change.

### ER-03 Safety controls have their own tests (high)

**Why it matters.** The tests that matter most are the ones where the agent should be stopped: the denied approval, the injected instruction, the path that escapes the workspace.

**What the scanner looks for.** Tests about prompt injection, jailbreaks, denied or expired approvals, forbidden tools, unauthorised access, path traversal, budget exhaustion.

- **Pass:** Three or more test files exercise refusals and attacks.
- **Partial:** One or two test files do.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** For every control in this scorecard, add a test that proves it blocks the bad case.

### ER-04 The agent can be stopped or rolled back (medium)

**Why it matters.** When an agent misbehaves in production you need to turn it off in seconds, or run it without side effects, without a deploy.

**What the scanner looks for.** Kill switches, feature flags, dry-run / simulation / shadow modes, circuit breakers, emergency stop; weaker: rollback, undo or checkpoints.

- **Pass:** A kill switch, flag or dry-run mode can disable or defang the agent.
- **Partial:** Actions can be rolled back or replayed from checkpoints, but not switched off.
- **Missing:** none of the above.

**Fix.** Add a runtime kill switch per agent and per tool tier, and a dry-run mode that records actions instead of executing them.
